The Lenape, whom the English called the Delaware, were an Algonquian people of the mid-Atlantic coast. Their homeland, Lenapehoking, covered what is now New Jersey, eastern Pennsylvania, Delaware and the lower Hudson valley, including Manhattan.

They lived in villages of related families, farmed maize, beans and squash, and fished the rivers and bays. The northern bands spoke Munsee and the southern bands Unami.

In the 1600s the Lenape traded furs with New Netherland and New Sweden, and lost many people to epidemics. In 1682 they made a treaty of friendship with William Penn, founder of Pennsylvania. Later Pennsylvania officials took a huge tract in the Walking Purchase of 1737. Pushed west step by step, Lenape groups moved to Ohio, Indiana, Kansas, Oklahoma and Ontario, where their descendants live today.
